stories.title: Washington Is About to Make the Energy Crisis a Whole Lot Worse
stories.text: Eight months into the US-Iran war, the Strait of Hormuz is still contested—and the oil shock nearly everyone predicted never arrived. Gregory Brew, senior energy analyst at Eurasia Group and a historian of modern Iran, explains why crude sits in the $90–$110 band instead of $250: alternative pipeline routes, high global inventories, a steep cut in Chinese imports, and an oil market practiced at absorbing shocks. He also breaks down the US escort operation moving 9 to 10 million barrels a day through the strait—supertankers running dark through the Omani channel—and why he calls it a Band-Aid. Also: the attack on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, Iranian production down to 2 million barrels a day, record US diesel prices ahead of the midterms, and why Brew expects Tehran to escalate rather than capitulate. stories.title: Trump’s AI Deregulator Has A Billion-Dollar Side Bet
stories.text: As David Sacks, President Donald Trump’s “ AI whisperer ,” urged the White House to take a light-touch approach to AI regulation, the tech tycoon’s venture capital firm launched a new round of investments in AI startups that stood to benefit from the looser rules. Since Sacks left his White House role in March — and concerns have mounted over AI’s potential harms — his firm, Craft Ventures, has continued pumping money into AI startups, including through a gargantuan new $1 billion fund. Sacks was not required to divest from the firm while serving in the Trump administration. Create a FREE account, or log in. stories.author: Judd Legum
stories.title: What congressional candidate Jay Feely really thinks about female athletes
stories.text: According to his campaign website, one of his top issues is “ protecting women’s sports .” According to Feely, “radical gender ideology is destroying fairness and opportunity for young women, and weak leaders are letting it happen.” Most of Feely’s commentary is geared toward excluding trans women from participating in women’s sports. This is largely a non-issue, as the NCAA has already limited participation in women’s athletics to “ student-athletes assigned female at birth ,” trans women are now barred from competing in women’s divisions in the Olympics, and there are no openly trans women competing in any professional sports in the United States. Most states, including Arizona, also ban trans girls from participating in girls sports. This raises the question as to why Feely has made the issue central to his campaign. Is he truly concerned about women’s sports? Or is he just interested in exploiting women’s athletics as a political cudgel? Unlike many congressional candidates, Feely has a lengthy history of public commentary before he entered the political arena. stories.text: Adam Hamilton, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, greets Jerilynn Henrikson on August 20, 2026 at Gravel City Roasters in Emporia, Ks. Henrikson said she is a lifelong Democrat and said, “I know I don’t want Marshall.” Photo: Clayton Steward Story by Clayton Steward and Justin Perkins Adam Hamilton, pastor and founder of Church of the Resurrection in the Kansas City suburbs, the largest United Methodist congregation in the United States, walked into a coffee shop in Emporia, Kansas, in late August. With a population of 24,000, Emporia is roughly the same size as Resurrection’s membership. But instead of preaching, Hamilton was there to make his case for why he can flip a seat for the U.S. Senate from the Sunflower State, a feat more than 90 years in the making. Hamilton told the crowd of about 40 people his campaign is rooted in his faith and experiences as a pastor but clarified that he is not running to force people to be Christian or United Methodist. Instead, he is motivated to uphold the U.S. Constitution and fight for individual rights.
